rungs.stem: The Tain Bo Cuailnge describes a physical transformation that comes over its young champion when he loses himself in combat: his body reshapes into something no longer human. Later Irish literature holds this passage as the signature battle-image of the whole tradition. Which hero undergoes it?
rungs.context: Fionn belongs to the later Fenian Cycle and never undergoes ristrad; Beowulf and Sigurd are heroes of other traditions listed here as adjacent distractors. Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: Cu Chulainn's battle-transformation has a specific Old Irish name -- a single word the Tain uses whenever the change comes on him. English translators have rendered it 'the warp-spasm' or 'the distortion'. What is the Old Irish word?
rungs.context: Also spelled riastradh. Geis = a magical prohibition; imbas = poetic inspiration; dinnshenchas = the lore of place-names. Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: The Tain's description of the transformation opens with the hero's body twisting inside its own skin. The lower half of each leg swings clean around and comes to rest facing the wrong way. Which specific pair of parts swaps?
choices: his feet swap to the back and his heels come to the front
his knees invert and his ankles snap outwards
his hips rotate a full turn inside their sockets
his ribs cave in and his spine bows the other way
rungs.answer: his feet swap to the back and his heels come to the front
rungs.context: The Tain says the body 'shook like a tree in flood'; feet and shins go behind, heels and calves in front. Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: Above the twisted body the Tain describes something rising straight from the crown of Cu Chulainn's head -- a column, described as taller than the mast of a ship, made either of dark blood or black smoke, visible from a distance to every warrior on the field. The Irish call it the LON LAITH. What is that in English?
rungs.context: Lon laith, sometimes 'warrior's moon'. A single black column above the crown -- his mark on any battlefield. Mythical Archives; Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: The Tain gives one specific detail about Cu Chulainn's eyes in the ristrad that has become one of the most-quoted images in Irish literature. One eye retreats -- so deep the text says a wild crane could not probe it out. The other eye does the opposite. What does the other eye do?
choices: it bulges out onto his cheek
it turns red as a hot coal
it closes and does not open
rungs.answer: it bulges out onto his cheek
rungs.context: One eye in, one eye out. One of the most reprinted passages in early Irish literature. Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: The Tain says Cu Chulainn's hair in the ristrad stands on end in a certain vivid way: sharp and stiff as the thorns of one specific plant, and each strand tipped with a spark of fire. The image is that a shaken apple tree's fruit would be spiked on his bristles rather than reach the ground. Which plant does the Tain name?
rungs.context: The 'red thornbush' of the passage is hawthorn -- the classic Irish quickthorn. Yew, oak, and ash are the other great sacred trees of Irish tradition, all real-adjacent distractors. Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: From Cu Chulainn's mouth in the ristrad the Tain gives one more sensory detail: his lower jaw strikes the upper 'a lion-killing blow' and out come objects as large as a ram's fleece each. What comes out?
rungs.context: The image is of the hero literally spitting fire the size of ram-fleeces. Wikipedia: Riastrad.

rungs.stem: Cu Chulainn's boyhood deeds close with a scene of practical horror: he comes back to Emain Macha from his first raid still in the ristrad, and the men of Ulster are so afraid he will slaughter them all that they will not open the gates. Conchobar's queen Mugain leads the women of the fort out to the plain. What do they do to shame him out of the frenzy?
choices: they walk out to meet him naked, baring their breasts
they set fire to their own hair in front of him
they lay their infant sons at his feet
they sing his mother's death-lament together
rungs.answer: they walk out to meet him naked, baring their breasts
rungs.context: Mugain leads the women out; Cu Chulainn covers his face at the sight -- the shame breaks the frenzy long enough for the warriors to seize him. Cuchulainn's Boyish Deeds (Tain Recension I).

rungs.stem: With the boy Cu Chulainn's face covered from the women, the warriors seize him and plunge him into a series of vats of cold water to cool the ristrad off him. The Tain reports what happens to each. FIRST vat: the water bursts the wooden staves. SECOND vat: the water boils with bubbles the size of a fist. What happens in the THIRD vat?
choices: the water heats only to a comfortable bath
the water freezes solid around him
the water is thrown out untouched
rungs.answer: the water heats only to a comfortable bath
rungs.context: First bursts, second boils, third tempers -- and the boy is himself again. Mugain then puts a blue mantle and silver brooch on him and seats him at Conchobar's knee. Cuchulainn's Boyish Deeds (Tain).

rungs.stem: The ristrad passage in the Tain is one of the longest sustained physical descriptions in early Irish literature -- a set-piece Old Irish scribes clearly relished. In which of the great medieval Irish codices does the fullest surviving version of the Tain (Recension II) appear?
choices: the Annals of the Four Masters
rungs.context: Lebor Laignech, c.1160. The Book of Kells is a gospel-book; the Cathach is a 6th-c. psalter; the Annals are 17th-c. history. Recension I is in the Lebor na hUidre. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

rungs.stem: Scholars often compare the ristrad to a related but distinct Norse battle-state: the frenzy of certain of Odin's warriors who shed their armour and fought in a trance, biting shields and howling. The Norse word for the state and the warriors is famous. What is it?
rungs.context: 'Going berserk'. Scholars note the ristrad is more monstrous and more visually elaborate than berserkergangr -- a physical melting into a fighting-shape, not merely a fury. Wergild = blood-price; einherjar = Odin's chosen dead; seidhr = Norse magic. Wikipedia: Berserker; Riastrad.

rungs.stem: The ristrad is the reason the Ulster Cycle can hold two facts about Cu Chulainn at once: in single combat he cannot be beaten, and in ordinary society he cannot be kept. It settles ONE argument about him decisively. Which one?
choices: why he alone can hold the ford against Medb's whole army
why he refuses the offered kingship of Ulster
why he leaves no living son to inherit his sword
why the Morrigan pursues him as a lover
rungs.answer: why he alone can hold the ford against Medb's whole army
rungs.context: The ristrad makes him unstoppable in single combat -- the one man who can hold the ford at Ath Fhirdiad. The other three are real Ulster Cycle threads but explained by other stories (Conchobar's kingship, Connla's death, the Morrigan's rebuff). Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge; Riastrad.
